services.summary: A managed video intelligence platform for registering streams, building continuous video-analysis applications, and retaining searchable metadata from live or batch video.
concepts: Streams represent video inputs; applications connect processors into a directed graph that transforms frames into annotations or events.
Warehouses retain ingested video and indexed intelligence so operators can search clips by time, source and detected attributes.
Occupancy analytics, person or vehicle recognition and custom models are deployed as processors rather than embedded into camera clients.
applicationFit: Use for multi-camera operational video where continuous ingestion, model execution and later search belong in one managed system.
Fit retail, manufacturing, safety and smart-space scenarios that need near-real-time alerts plus historical investigation.
Use Vision API or Video Intelligence API instead when the workload is a stateless image request or asynchronous file annotation job.

architectureFlows.title: Continuous camera analytics
architectureFlows.note: RTSP feeds enter registered streams, an application graph evaluates frames and events are delivered to an operational consumer.

architectureFlows.title: Searchable video warehouse
architectureFlows.note: Stored video and annotations are indexed for investigators without replaying every source file.

security: Use dedicated service accounts for ingestion, application deployment and warehouse search; camera credentials should not be shared with analysts.
Place event consumers behind least-privilege Pub/Sub subscriptions and treat face, person and license-plate metadata as sensitive data.
Define regional residency, retention and deletion controls before ingesting regulated surveillance video; audit both configuration and search access.
operations: Monitor stream connectivity, dropped frames, processor latency and application health separately so camera faults are not mistaken for model faults.
Version application graphs and models, canary new processors on representative streams and validate event precision before broad rollout.
Set warehouse retention and export procedures, then rehearse recovery from stream credential rotation and regional input loss.
watchPoints: Source codecs, frame rates and network stability directly affect usable inference; validate supported media profiles at the edge.
Continuous video can create high storage and inference volume; apply sampling and retention based on the actual detection objective.
A recognized object is model output, not identity proof; include confidence thresholds and human review for consequential decisions.
cost: Charges are driven by video ingestion/processing duration, model or application execution and retained warehouse data.
Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, logging and network egress used around the platform add separate charges.
Estimate using cameras × active hours × sampled frame rate, then add retention and event-consumer costs.
alternatives: Agent Platform Vision — Continuous stream graphs and searchable video warehouses.
Video Intelligence API — Asynchronous or streaming annotation through an API.
Vision API — Stateless analysis of individual images.

comparisons.name: Agent Platform Vision
comparisons.fit: Continuous stream graphs and searchable video warehouses.

comparisons.name: Video Intelligence API
comparisons.fit: Asynchronous or streaming annotation through an API.

comparisons.name: Vision API
comparisons.fit: Stateless analysis of individual images.

memoryHooks: Stream → application graph → events; warehouse → indexed search.
Continuous camera estate points to Agent Platform Vision, not a one-file annotation API.
Certification clue: managed live-video ingestion plus retained searchable intelligence.

services.summary: Google-designed tensor accelerators delivered as TPU VMs or queued resources for high-throughput training and inference with XLA-based frameworks.
concepts: A TPU chip contains matrix multiply units optimized for dense tensor operations; chips are connected as slices or large multislice topologies.
TPU VMs give direct host access, while queued resources request capacity that is provisioned when the selected accelerator topology becomes available.
JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch/XLA compile graphs through XLA; model shape, precision and input pipeline determine utilization.
applicationFit: Choose TPUs for transformer, vision and scientific models that scale across many identical accelerator cores.
Use reservations or queued resources for planned large training runs; use Spot TPUs only for checkpointable work.
Prefer GPUs when libraries depend on CUDA-specific kernels or the workload cannot efficiently compile/vectorize through XLA.

architectureFlows.title: Distributed TPU training
architectureFlows.note: Training data is staged close to the accelerator, workers compile the graph and checkpoints leave the TPU lifecycle boundary.

architectureFlows.title: Capacity-aware training queue
architectureFlows.note: A queued resource waits for a complete topology so a distributed job starts with coherent capacity.

security: Assign the TPU VM service account only dataset, artifact and logging permissions required by the job.
Use private IP networking and VPC controls where supported; restrict SSH and OS access to managed administrator paths.
Protect training data and checkpoints with Cloud Storage IAM and CMEK where required, recognizing host/runtime configuration has separate controls.
operations: Track MXU utilization, host CPU, input wait time, HBM pressure and compile time; low accelerator use often originates in the data pipeline.
Checkpoint to durable storage at a frequency matched to Spot/preemption risk and the time required to rebuild the TPU topology.
Pin framework and TPU software versions, test numerical behavior when changing precision, and delete idle slices after jobs finish.
watchPoints: TPU type, topology and region must be selected together; quota alone does not guarantee immediate physical capacity.
Code that runs on one device may need explicit sharding and collective-operation changes to scale efficiently.
Large slices fail economically when input data, batch size or checkpoint throughput cannot feed the accelerator fabric.
cost: Billing follows accelerator type, chip count and provisioned duration; on-demand, reservation and Spot economics differ.
TPU VMs, persistent disks, Cloud Storage operations and cross-region data transfer are additional cost components.
Compare time-to-train and achieved utilization, not hourly accelerator price alone.
alternatives: Cloud TPU — XLA-friendly models needing Google tensor accelerators.
GPU VM / GKE GPU — CUDA ecosystems, custom kernels and broad framework compatibility.
Vertex AI custom training — Managed job orchestration that can consume TPU or GPU resources.

comparisons.name: Cloud TPU
comparisons.fit: XLA-friendly models needing Google tensor accelerators.

comparisons.name: GPU VM / GKE GPU
comparisons.fit: CUDA ecosystems, custom kernels and broad framework compatibility.

comparisons.name: Vertex AI custom training
comparisons.fit: Managed job orchestration that can consume TPU or GPU resources.

memoryHooks: TPU performance is a compiler, topology and input-pipeline problem—not just a faster VM.
Queued resources solve coordinated TPU capacity; checkpoints solve interruption.
Exam clue: large JAX/TensorFlow training with dense tensor math and XLA points to TPU.

consoleSteps.detail: Console → Compute Engine → TPUs; confirm region/zone, TPU type, topology and project quota.

consoleSteps.title: Create the resource
consoleSteps.detail: Create a TPU VM or queued resource, selecting runtime version, network, service account and SSH policy.

consoleSteps.title: Connect the workload
consoleSteps.detail: Use SSH/IAP or a managed training job, stage data in Cloud Storage and compile the model with XLA.

consoleSteps.title: Observe and release
consoleSteps.detail: Inspect TPU utilization and job logs, confirm checkpoints, then delete the slice/queued resource when complete.

services.summary: A managed, collaborative notebook environment integrated with Vertex AI that supplies governed runtimes, sharing and Google Cloud data access without local notebook servers.
concepts: A notebook file is a collaborative artifact; its runtime is a separate regional compute resource with machine type, accelerator and idle-shutdown settings.
Managed runtimes run in the user's project and use Google Cloud identity, IAM and audit controls rather than personal Colab consumer storage.
BigQuery and Cloud Storage integrations let analysts work close to governed data while notebook execution remains reproducible through runtime templates.
applicationFit: Use for interactive exploration, teaching and model prototyping where browser collaboration and enterprise governance matter.
Choose shared runtime templates when platform teams must standardize machine types, networks, packages and idle controls.
Use Vertex AI Workbench when teams require a more persistent Jupyter environment, deeper environment customization or managed notebook instances.

architectureFlows.title: Governed analytics notebook
architectureFlows.note: An analyst opens a shared notebook, starts a controlled runtime and queries governed data without copying it to a laptop.

architectureFlows.title: Prototype-to-training handoff
architectureFlows.note: Exploratory code is validated in a notebook, then moved to repeatable managed training and an artifact registry.

security: Separate notebook-sharing permission from data permissions; access to a notebook must not automatically grant access to BigQuery tables or buckets.
Use runtime service accounts and network templates with least privilege; avoid embedding keys or tokens in cells and outputs.
Apply VPC Service Controls/CMEK where supported and clear sensitive outputs before sharing notebook artifacts broadly.
operations: Enforce idle shutdown, approved runtime templates and quota limits so abandoned sessions do not become permanent compute.
Version important notebooks in source control or export repeatable code into pipelines; collaborative history is not a production release process.
Monitor runtime creation failures, accelerator quota, package drift and long-running cells; document ownership of shared notebooks.
watchPoints: Notebook region and runtime region affect data locality and available machine types.
A stopped or deleted runtime does not equal a deleted notebook; manage artifact and compute lifecycles independently.
Interactive success does not prove batch reproducibility—pin packages, seeds, data snapshots and service-account permissions.
cost: Runtime VM/accelerator uptime is the primary cost; BigQuery queries, storage and network transfer are billed separately.
Idle shutdown and smaller default templates provide the largest control for exploratory workloads.
Chargeback should attribute runtime labels and downstream data-processing jobs, not only notebook count.
alternatives: Colab Enterprise — Collaborative browser notebooks with managed enterprise runtimes.
Vertex AI Workbench — Persistent Jupyter development environment with deeper customization.
Vertex AI Pipelines — Repeatable, scheduled and lineage-aware ML workflows.

comparisons.name: Colab Enterprise
comparisons.fit: Collaborative browser notebooks with managed enterprise runtimes.

comparisons.name: Vertex AI Workbench
comparisons.fit: Persistent Jupyter development environment with deeper customization.

comparisons.name: Vertex AI Pipelines
comparisons.fit: Repeatable, scheduled and lineage-aware ML workflows.

memoryHooks: Notebook is the shared document; runtime is the billable execution resource.
Use Colab for exploration, then move repeatable work to training jobs or pipelines.
Exam clue: familiar Colab collaboration under IAM and Vertex AI governance.

consoleSteps.detail: Share the notebook separately from its data, review runtime inventory and stop/delete idle compute.

services.summary: Google-maintained container images with preinstalled ML frameworks, CUDA libraries and common tooling for reproducible training, inference and notebook workloads.
concepts: Images are framework/version-specific and published in Artifact Registry; CPU, GPU and accelerator variants have different drivers and libraries.
A container fixes the user-space ML stack, while the host or managed service still supplies compatible accelerator drivers, identity and networking.
Release tags can move; immutable digests provide repeatable builds and make vulnerability findings traceable to an exact base image.
applicationFit: Use when the same curated framework stack must run across Vertex AI, GKE, Compute Engine or local development.
Choose a GPU image only when the target runtime supplies compatible NVIDIA hardware and drivers.
Build a custom derivative when extra packages are required, but retain the supported base and scan the resulting image.

architectureFlows.title: Managed training image
architectureFlows.note: A versioned image moves from registry through a Vertex AI custom job to durable model artifacts.

architectureFlows.title: Portable GPU workload
architectureFlows.note: The same digest is tested on a workstation and scheduled on GKE with host drivers exposed through the device plugin.

security: Grant pull access only to runtime identities and keep image-push rights in the build pipeline.
Use Artifact Analysis scanning, provenance and Binary Authorization for derived production images.
Never bake datasets, credentials or service-account keys into layers; mount or fetch them at runtime through IAM.
operations: Track published image support and framework/CUDA compatibility before updating a tag.
Rebuild derivatives regularly to inherit patched base layers, then run model regression and accelerator smoke tests.
Record image digest with every experiment and endpoint release so rollback restores both code and framework.
watchPoints: A container image does not install or manage host GPU drivers.
Adding arbitrary packages can break the tested framework/CUDA combination and removes some support assumptions.
Public image availability does not grant workload access to private data; runtime IAM remains separate.
cost: Images themselves are available as artifacts; charges come from Artifact Registry storage/egress, builds and the compute running them.
Large ML layers increase build, pull and node-start time, which matters for elastic clusters.
Reuse regional registries and layered builds to reduce transfer and rebuild overhead.
alternatives: Deep Learning Containers — Portable, curated containerized ML runtime.
Deep Learning VM — Curated ML stack delivered as a VM image.
Custom container — Maximum package control with full maintenance responsibility.

comparisons.fit: Portable, curated containerized ML runtime.

comparisons.name: Deep Learning VM
comparisons.fit: Curated ML stack delivered as a VM image.

memoryHooks: Container controls user space; host controls drivers and hardware.
Pin digest, scan derivative, record it with the model.
Exam clue: consistent framework environment across GKE, Vertex AI and VMs.

services.summary: Compute Engine VM images preconfigured with ML frameworks, accelerator drivers and notebook tooling for customizable deep-learning development and training.
concepts: Images bundle an operating system, framework and accelerator software; image family and release determine compatibility and patch baseline.
The resource is still a Compute Engine VM, so machine type, disks, network, Shielded VM settings and service account remain customer design choices.
GPU attachment needs quota and a compatible image/driver; startup scripts can add packages but also introduce configuration drift.
applicationFit: Use for SSH/Jupyter-based research that needs root-level VM customization or software not supported by managed notebooks.
Choose it for long-lived development hosts and special drivers; use managed training jobs for repeatable ephemeral runs.
Prefer Deep Learning Containers when portability across orchestrators is more important than full VM control.

architectureFlows.title: Private research workstation
architectureFlows.note: A researcher reaches a hardened VM through IAP while datasets stay in private Google Cloud services.

architectureFlows.title: Reproducible VM training pool
architectureFlows.note: An instance template pins the image and startup configuration so disposable workers recreate the same environment.

security: Use OS Login and IAP instead of public SSH, and remove broad cloud-platform access from the VM service account.
Keep secrets outside notebooks and startup scripts; retrieve them with Secret Manager and workload identity.
Patch the OS and framework image, scan installed packages and use Shielded VM controls where workload compatibility allows.
operations: Monitor GPU utilization, disk throughput, memory and idle time; stop schedules or instance policies should handle abandoned workstations.
Recreate from a pinned image/template rather than repairing snowflake VMs; persist code and results outside the boot disk.
Test driver/framework changes with representative models before rotating an image family in templates.
watchPoints: Image-family references can advance to a newer release; pin a specific image for regulated or reproducible builds.
Stopping a VM preserves disks and may retain accelerator reservation implications; it does not eliminate every storage cost.
Notebook access, OS access and Google Cloud API access are separate identity surfaces.
cost: Compute Engine VM, GPU/TPU attachment, disks, snapshots and network egress are billed independently.
Committed use discounts or reservations suit steady research fleets; Spot suits checkpointable training.
Idle GPU time dominates cost, so schedule shutdown and expose utilization to project owners.
alternatives: Deep Learning VM — Customizable VM with curated ML software.
Deep Learning Containers — Portable curated runtime on an existing host/orchestrator.
Colab Enterprise — Collaborative managed notebook with less host administration.

comparisons.fit: Customizable VM with curated ML software.

comparisons.name: Deep Learning Containers
comparisons.fit: Portable curated runtime on an existing host/orchestrator.

comparisons.fit: Collaborative managed notebook with less host administration.

memoryHooks: Curated image does not remove Compute Engine administration.
Persist artifacts externally; rebuild the VM from a pinned definition.

services.summary: A natural-language understanding platform for intent-based chat and voice agents built from agents, intents, entities, contexts and fulfillment webhooks.
concepts: An agent owns intents and entity types; training phrases map utterances to intents and parameters extracted from system or custom entities.
Input/output contexts carry conversational state across turns and control which intents are eligible to match.
Fulfillment can return static responses or call a webhook; telephony and messaging integrations provide channels but do not replace backend business logic.
applicationFit: Use for small-to-medium intent-driven bots with relatively linear conversations and established ES integrations.
Choose CX for complex state machines, reusable flows, large teams and explicit page/route control.
Use a generative agent platform when free-form reasoning and tool use dominate over deterministic intent routing.

architectureFlows.title: Transactional chat bot
architectureFlows.note: A channel sends text to the ES agent, which extracts parameters and invokes a protected fulfillment service.

architectureFlows.title: Voice self-service
architectureFlows.note: Telephony audio is transcribed, routed through intents and escalated with session context when automation cannot complete.

security: Authenticate fulfillment with service-to-service identity, validate parameters server-side and never trust a matched intent as authorization.
Limit agent editors and export access because training phrases can contain sensitive utterances and business vocabulary.
Configure logging, retention and regionalization according to conversation-data policy; redact sensitive values before downstream logs.
operations: Measure intent match, fallback, no-input, webhook latency/error and containment by journey—not only total sessions.
Use versions/environments for controlled promotion and automated conversation tests for critical intents.
Review unmatched utterances to improve phrases/entities while preventing overfitting and ambiguous intent overlap.
watchPoints: Contexts are session-scoped state, not a durable customer database.
Webhook deadlines require fast backends and graceful retry/idempotency behavior.
Built-in integrations vary by region and channel; verify lifecycle and support before architecture commitment.
cost: Pricing commonly follows text/audio requests or session usage; telephony, Speech APIs and backend compute can add charges.
Verbose logging and retained conversation exports create separate observability/storage cost.
Estimate by turns per conversation and audio duration, not monthly user count alone.
alternatives: Dialogflow ES — Intent/context bot with moderate conversation complexity.
Dialogflow CX — Explicit flows/pages for complex enterprise journeys.
Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform — Generative enterprise agents, grounding and tool orchestration.

comparisons.name: Dialogflow ES
comparisons.fit: Intent/context bot with moderate conversation complexity.

comparisons.name: Dialogflow CX
comparisons.fit: Explicit flows/pages for complex enterprise journeys.

comparisons.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
comparisons.fit: Generative enterprise agents, grounding and tool orchestration.

memoryHooks: Intent says what; entity extracts values; context carries turn state; webhook performs the action.
ES favors intent-centric flows; CX favors explicit state-machine design.
Exam clue: established FAQ/transaction bot with intents and contexts.

services.summary: Document AI converts unstructured documents into structured text and entities through OCR, pretrained or custom processors and human-review-aware workflows.
concepts: A processor is a regional endpoint configured for a document task such as OCR, invoices, forms or custom extraction; processor versions control model behavior.
Online processing handles synchronous documents while batch processing reads and writes Cloud Storage for larger asynchronous workloads.
The Document response carries page layout, text anchors, entities, confidence and normalized values—not merely plain OCR text.
applicationFit: Use for invoices, IDs, contracts and forms where layout-aware extraction and normalized business fields matter.
Select pretrained processors when schemas match; use custom extractor/classifier models for organization-specific documents.
Use Vision OCR for simpler image-to-text tasks that do not need document processors or structured entities.

architectureFlows.title: Invoice processing pipeline
architectureFlows.note: Documents land in a controlled bucket, a processor extracts normalized fields and low-confidence cases enter review.

architectureFlows.title: Batch document migration
architectureFlows.note: A manifest drives asynchronous processing and results are partitioned for analytics and search.

security: Keep processor, input bucket and output bucket in compatible regions and grant the runtime identity only object and processor-use permissions.
Treat extracted text and entities as the same sensitivity as source documents; apply CMEK/VPC Service Controls where supported.
Prevent prompt or document content from becoming executable instructions in downstream automation; validate extracted values against systems of record.
operations: Track processor version, confidence distribution, field-level precision/recall, page failures and human correction rate.
Deploy a new processor version behind a representative evaluation set and preserve the previous version for rollback.
Use idempotent document IDs and output paths so retries do not create duplicate business transactions.
watchPoints: File type, page count, size and synchronous limits differ; batch large documents rather than forcing online processing.
OCR confidence is not business validity—totals, dates and identifiers still need domain checks.
Processor availability and data residency are regional; moving documents across regions can violate policy and add transfer cost.
cost: Billing is usually per page and depends on processor type; custom training/hosting and human review can add costs.
Cloud Storage operations, batch orchestration, BigQuery analysis and egress are separate.
Reduce cost by classifying/routing documents before expensive specialized extraction and by avoiding duplicate reprocessing.
alternatives: Document AI — Layout-aware document processors and structured entities.
Vision API OCR — General image/PDF text detection without business document schemas.
Custom ML pipeline — Full model control with larger training and operations burden.

comparisons.name: Document AI
comparisons.fit: Layout-aware document processors and structured entities.

comparisons.name: Vision API OCR
comparisons.fit: General image/PDF text detection without business document schemas.

comparisons.name: Custom ML pipeline
comparisons.fit: Full model control with larger training and operations burden.

memoryHooks: Processor + version + region define the extraction contract.
Confidence routes work; validation authorizes business action.
Exam clue: invoices/forms requiring fields, tables and normalized values.

services.summary: A managed capability for turning enterprise data into connected entities and relationships that improve discovery, semantic context and grounded applications.
concepts: A knowledge graph models entities, attributes and typed relationships so applications can traverse meaning rather than join only by literal keys.
Entity resolution reconciles aliases and duplicate records into canonical identities while preserving provenance to source systems.
Ontology and schema governance determine which concepts and relationships are trustworthy enough for search, analytics or agent grounding.
applicationFit: Use when customer, product, asset or supplier data spans systems and relationship context is central to the question.
Fit semantic search and grounded-agent scenarios that need curated enterprise facts with provenance.
Do not introduce a graph for simple tabular reporting where BigQuery joins and governed dimensions are sufficient.

architectureFlows.title: Enterprise entity graph
architectureFlows.note: Source records are normalized, resolved to canonical entities and published with provenance for downstream consumers.

architectureFlows.title: Grounded assistant retrieval
architectureFlows.note: A user question resolves relevant entities and relationships before selected facts are supplied to a model.

security: Apply source-system entitlements during graph retrieval; a connected graph must not flatten access boundaries.
Retain provenance and change history so merged identities and inferred relationships can be challenged or corrected.
Classify sensitive relationship data and prevent high-risk inferences from being exposed merely because individual records were readable.
operations: Measure match/merge precision, orphan entities, stale sources, schema violations and query latency.
Establish ontology ownership and a correction workflow; uncontrolled relationship types quickly erode trust.
Version ingestion mappings and backfill carefully when canonical IDs or merge rules change.
watchPoints: False-positive entity merges are often more damaging than duplicates because they combine unrelated data and permissions.
Graph freshness is bounded by source ingestion and resolution cadence; state it in consuming applications.
A knowledge graph supplies facts and relationships, not automatic authorization or model truthfulness.
cost: Cost follows ingestion/processing, graph storage, queries and connected pipelines or model calls.
High-cardinality relationships and frequent full rebuilds increase processing and validation expense.
Compare the operational value of relationship traversal with a governed BigQuery semantic model before choosing graph architecture.
alternatives: Enterprise Knowledge Graph — Curated entities and relationships for semantic enterprise use.
BigQuery — Large-scale SQL analytics and governed dimensional models.
Vertex AI Search / agent grounding — Retrieval experience that can consume curated enterprise knowledge.

comparisons.name: Enterprise Knowledge Graph
comparisons.fit: Curated entities and relationships for semantic enterprise use.

comparisons.name: BigQuery
comparisons.fit: Large-scale SQL analytics and governed dimensional models.

comparisons.name: Vertex AI Search / agent grounding
comparisons.fit: Retrieval experience that can consume curated enterprise knowledge.

memoryHooks: Resolve identity before traversing relationships; keep provenance with every fact.
A graph connects meaning, but entitlements still filter every retrieval.
Exam clue: fragmented enterprise records plus relationship-aware discovery.

consoleSteps.detail: From the product console/project, establish entity types, identifiers, relationships and provenance requirements.

services.summary: An enterprise agent platform for creating grounded Gemini-powered assistants that search organizational content, invoke approved tools and operate under enterprise identity controls.
concepts: Agents combine model instructions, enterprise data stores and tools; grounding retrieves authorized evidence at request time instead of relying only on model memory.
Connectors index content from supported repositories while ACL-aware retrieval is required to preserve source permissions.
Tool calls move an agent from answering to acting, so schemas, confirmation rules and transaction boundaries become part of security design.
applicationFit: Use for employee assistants, research and cross-system workflows that need enterprise search plus conversational reasoning.
Choose deterministic orchestration such as Workflows for fixed business processes where every transition must be predefined.
Use a narrow API such as Translation or Speech-to-Text when the task is a single transformation rather than an agentic workflow.

architectureFlows.title: ACL-aware enterprise assistant
architectureFlows.note: A signed-in employee retrieves permitted evidence, Gemini produces a cited response and feedback feeds quality operations.

architectureFlows.title: Action-taking support agent
architectureFlows.note: The agent retrieves policy, proposes an action and invokes a backend only after policy and confirmation gates succeed.

security: Propagate user identity to retrieval and tools; never let a broadly privileged indexing or tool account silently bypass source ACLs.
Separate read tools from mutating tools, require confirmation for consequential actions and validate every tool argument server-side.
Apply data-store, conversation-retention, model-safety and audit policies; defend retrieval content against prompt injection.
operations: Evaluate groundedness, citation quality, retrieval recall, task completion, tool error and unsafe-action rate on a curated test set.
Version instructions, connector configuration and tools together; canary changes and keep trace data sufficient to diagnose regressions.
Monitor connector freshness and permission synchronization because stale indexes can create inaccurate or unauthorized answers.
watchPoints: A citation shows retrieval provenance, not that the source is correct or current.
Connector ingestion and ACL sync have latency; design revocation expectations explicitly.
Generative output is probabilistic—high-impact decisions need deterministic validation or human approval.
cost: Costs can include indexed data/search, model input/output tokens, connector processing and tool backends.
Long contexts and repeated retrieval increase latency and token charges; retrieve the smallest evidence set that answers the task.
Measure cost per successfully completed task, not only cost per chat turn.
alternatives: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform — Grounded enterprise assistants with connectors and tools.
Dialogflow ES — Intent-driven conversational automation.
Workflows — Deterministic service orchestration without generative reasoning.

comparisons.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
comparisons.fit: Grounded enterprise assistants with connectors and tools.

comparisons.name: Dialogflow ES
comparisons.fit: Intent-driven conversational automation.

comparisons.name: Workflows
comparisons.fit: Deterministic service orchestration without generative reasoning.

memoryHooks: Grounding answers with evidence; tools turn evidence into controlled action.
User ACLs must survive indexing, retrieval and tool execution.
Exam clue: enterprise assistant searching internal content and invoking governed tools.

consoleSteps.detail: Console → Gemini Enterprise; create an app/agent in the intended project and location.

consoleSteps.title: Add enterprise data
consoleSteps.detail: Configure supported connectors/data stores, synchronization cadence and ACL-aware identity mapping.

services.summary: A managed live-video transcoding service that converts real-time input feeds into adaptive-bitrate HLS or DASH renditions for delivery through Cloud Storage and a CDN.
concepts: An input endpoint accepts live SRT or RTMP contribution; a channel defines elementary streams, muxed outputs, manifests and the output bucket.
Adaptive bitrate ladders create multiple resolution/bitrate renditions so players switch based on device and network conditions.
The service writes manifests and segments to Cloud Storage; CDN delivery and playback authorization remain separate architecture layers.
applicationFit: Use for 24×7 or event live streaming that needs managed transcoding and packaged HLS/DASH output.
Combine with Media CDN or Cloud CDN for global audience distribution and origin protection.
Use Transcoder API for file-based video-on-demand assets, not an ongoing live contribution feed.

architectureFlows.title: Global live event
architectureFlows.note: An encoder contributes one reliable feed; Live Stream API produces renditions that a CDN distributes globally.

architectureFlows.title: Protected premium stream
architectureFlows.note: Playback requests are authorized at the edge while segments originate from a restricted output bucket.

security: Restrict input endpoint details and permit output-bucket writes only to the service agent; viewers should access content through the delivery layer.
Use signed requests/tokens and DRM or application entitlement controls where content rights require them.
Separate contribution-network access, channel administration and playback authorization into different identities and audit trails.
operations: Monitor input continuity, channel state, encoding errors, segment freshness and end-to-end player latency.
Start and stop channels through a rehearsed event runbook and validate every rendition/manifest before audience cutover.
Use redundant encoders and contribution paths for premium events; archive the source separately if replay or forensic recovery is required.
watchPoints: Starting a channel without a valid continuous input does not create useful output and can still consume provisioned resources.
Codec, frame rate, keyframe interval and audio layout must be compatible with the selected transcoding ladder.
Live Stream API creates media outputs; it does not provide a player, subscriber system or complete DRM service.
cost: Charges depend on channel transcoding time and output characteristics; HD/UHD and multiple renditions increase processing.
Cloud Storage, CDN delivery, cache misses, logging and network egress are separate charges.
For events, automate channel start/stop and choose the smallest ladder that meets device and quality requirements.
alternatives: Live Stream API — Real-time input to live HLS/DASH outputs.
Transcoder API — Asynchronous file-to-file VOD transcoding.
Video Stitcher API — Server-side ad insertion into live or VOD manifests.

comparisons.fit: Real-time input to live HLS/DASH outputs.

comparisons.name: Transcoder API
comparisons.fit: Asynchronous file-to-file VOD transcoding.

comparisons.name: Video Stitcher API
comparisons.fit: Server-side ad insertion into live or VOD manifests.

memoryHooks: Input endpoint receives; channel transcodes; bucket originates; CDN delivers.
Live Stream creates renditions, Video Stitcher personalizes manifests.

services.summary: A speech recognition API for converting short, long-form or streaming audio into transcripts with language, model, adaptation and diarization controls.
concepts: Synchronous recognition suits short audio, batch recognition processes stored files, and streaming recognition returns interim/final results over a live connection.
Recognizer configuration selects language, model and features; phrase adaptation biases likely vocabulary but does not guarantee a phrase.
Word time offsets, confidence, punctuation, channel separation and diarization enrich transcripts for downstream workflows.
applicationFit: Use for call transcription, captions, voice commands and searchable media where audio must become text.
Use streaming for interactive latency and batch for throughput-oriented stored audio.
Pair with Dialogflow when transcription is only the input stage of an intent-based conversation.

architectureFlows.title: Contact-center transcription
architectureFlows.note: Separate audio channels are streamed or batched into transcripts that are redacted and analyzed.

architectureFlows.title: Real-time captions
architectureFlows.note: A client streams correctly encoded audio, receives interim hypotheses and displays only stable final segments.

security: Send audio only from authenticated workloads and restrict access to stored recordings/transcripts separately.
Treat voice and transcripts as sensitive personal data; apply consent, retention, residency and redaction requirements.
Avoid logging raw audio or credentials in request diagnostics; use service accounts and private access controls where applicable.
operations: Measure word error rate on domain audio, end-to-end latency, empty results, stream reconnects and quota exhaustion.
Keep an evaluation corpus across accents, codecs and noise conditions before changing models or adaptation.
Retry batch jobs idempotently; streaming clients must handle session limits and reconnect without duplicating finalized text.
watchPoints: Declared encoding and sample rate must match the actual audio or accuracy can collapse without a clear API error.
Diarization estimates speakers; multi-channel recognition is preferable when speakers are already isolated.
Confidence is model evidence, not a universal probability or authorization signal.
cost: Billing is based primarily on audio duration and selected recognition features/model.
Storage, streaming transport, redaction, analytics and egress add downstream costs.
Trim silence, choose the correct model and avoid retranscribing unchanged recordings.
alternatives: Speech-to-Text — General audio transcription with streaming and batch modes.
Dialogflow ES — Conversation intent/entity handling after speech recognition.
Video Intelligence API — Video annotation where speech transcription is one media feature.

comparisons.name: Speech-to-Text
comparisons.fit: General audio transcription with streaming and batch modes.

comparisons.name: Dialogflow ES
comparisons.fit: Conversation intent/entity handling after speech recognition.

comparisons.name: Video Intelligence API
comparisons.fit: Video annotation where speech transcription is one media feature.

memoryHooks: Audio configuration must describe the bytes actually sent.
Streaming favors latency; batch favors stored-audio throughput.
Exam clue: convert calls or microphone audio to timestamped text.

services.summary: An enterprise support and compatibility offering for selected TensorFlow versions on Google Cloud, aimed at stable production ML environments rather than a separate execution service.
concepts: TensorFlow Enterprise centers on supported TensorFlow distributions and long maintenance windows for designated versions.
The framework still runs on Compute Engine, GKE, Deep Learning images or managed training; TensorFlow Enterprise does not create a new data plane.
Compatibility with CUDA, cuDNN, Python and accelerator drivers must be validated as one tested runtime stack.
applicationFit: Use when production TensorFlow workloads need a curated, supportable version strategy on Google Cloud.
Combine with Deep Learning Containers/VM images to consume tested framework and accelerator combinations.
Do not select it as an inference endpoint or training scheduler; use Vertex AI, GKE or Compute Engine for runtime orchestration.

architectureFlows.title: Supported TensorFlow training stack
architectureFlows.note: A pinned supported image moves through testing into managed training with exact dependencies recorded.

architectureFlows.title: Long-lived inference maintenance
architectureFlows.note: A production model and runtime are upgraded independently through a compatibility matrix and canary deployment.

security: Scan and sign images containing the framework, and isolate runtime service accounts from build identities.
Patch the full image/OS stack; a supported TensorFlow package does not remediate vulnerable system or Python dependencies.
Protect model artifacts and training data through the storage and runtime platform's IAM/CMEK controls.
operations: Maintain a compatibility matrix for TensorFlow, Python, CUDA/cuDNN, drivers, hardware and model format.
Capture exact package/image versions and run numerical, performance and serialization regression tests before upgrades.
Track end-of-support dates and plan migration rather than allowing production jobs to depend indefinitely on an obsolete version.
watchPoints: Framework support does not guarantee that custom ops or third-party packages work after an upgrade.
The catalog name can be mistaken for a standalone managed service; architecture must still name the actual compute/training platform.
SavedModel and custom-op compatibility deserve explicit rollback tests across runtime versions.
cost: Framework packages are not the main billable resource; compute accelerators, storage, images and support plan drive cost.
Staying on a supported stack can reduce engineering risk but may constrain adoption of the newest framework release.
Account for duplicate environments during upgrade and performance validation.
alternatives: TensorFlow Enterprise — Supported TensorFlow version strategy on Google Cloud.
Deep Learning Containers — Curated runnable image, including framework dependencies.
Vertex AI training — Managed orchestration and infrastructure for training jobs.

comparisons.fit: Supported TensorFlow version strategy on Google Cloud.

comparisons.name: Deep Learning Containers
comparisons.fit: Curated runnable image, including framework dependencies.

comparisons.name: Vertex AI training
comparisons.fit: Managed orchestration and infrastructure for training jobs.

memoryHooks: It is a supported framework stack, not a training control plane.
Version TensorFlow, CUDA, driver and model compatibility together.
Exam clue: production TensorFlow stability and extended support.

consoleSteps.title: Run compatibility tests
consoleSteps.detail: Validate custom ops, SavedModel load, numerical results and accelerator performance.

consoleSteps.title: Promote with evidence
consoleSteps.detail: Record exact image/package versions, canary the new runtime and retain a tested rollback image.

services.summary: A speech synthesis API that converts text or SSML into natural-sounding audio using selectable languages, voices, encodings and speaking controls.
concepts: Input can be plain text or SSML; SSML adds pauses, pronunciation, emphasis and other presentation controls.
Voice selection combines language, named voice and model family; audio configuration defines encoding, pitch, speaking rate and effects profile.
Synthesis returns audio bytes or long-form output depending on method; the application owns playback, caching and content workflow.
applicationFit: Use for accessibility narration, IVR prompts, learning content and dynamic spoken responses.
Pre-synthesize stable phrases and cache them; synthesize personalized or rapidly changing text on demand.
Use human voice production where brand performance, legal approval or highly expressive direction outweighs dynamic generation.

architectureFlows.title: Accessible content narration
architectureFlows.note: Approved text is normalized, synthesized once and cached for repeated delivery.

architectureFlows.title: Conversational voice response
architectureFlows.note: A bot response is policy-filtered, converted to low-latency audio and returned through a telephony or app channel.

security: Restrict synthesis to trusted workloads to prevent abuse, unexpected cost or generation of unauthorized content.
Do not send secrets or unnecessary personal data in synthesis text; logs and caches must follow the text's classification.
Confirm voice usage, disclosure and consent requirements for the target geography and experience.
operations: Monitor characters synthesized, latency, quota errors, unsupported SSML and playback failures by voice/locale.
Regression-test pronunciation dictionaries and SSML when changing voices; voice names and capabilities are not interchangeable.
Cache immutable audio by normalized-text, voice and configuration hash so a voice change does not serve stale output.
watchPoints: SSML must be valid and within request limits; unsupported tags or excessive input require chunking and validation.
Audio encoding must match the playback channel—telephony and web clients often need different formats.
A natural voice does not verify the underlying text; content correctness is upstream responsibility.
cost: Billing is primarily based on characters synthesized and voice/model class.
Cloud Storage, CDN delivery and application compute are separate; caching repeated prompts can materially reduce calls.
Estimate by normalized character count, languages and premium voice selection rather than number of audio files.
alternatives: Text-to-Speech — Dynamic text/SSML synthesis into audio.
Recorded human audio — Highest directed performance for stable content.
Speech-to-Text — The inverse task: audio into text.

comparisons.name: Text-to-Speech
comparisons.fit: Dynamic text/SSML synthesis into audio.

comparisons.name: Recorded human audio
comparisons.fit: Highest directed performance for stable content.

comparisons.name: Speech-to-Text
comparisons.fit: The inverse task: audio into text.

memoryHooks: Text/SSML in; encoded audio out; playback remains your application.
Cache stable prompts and key cache by voice configuration.
Exam clue: generate multilingual spoken audio from application text.

services.summary: An asynchronous media transcoding service that converts Cloud Storage video files into web-ready renditions, manifests, thumbnails and other VOD outputs.
concepts: A job references an input URI, output URI and job template or inline configuration; processing is regional and asynchronous.
Elementary streams define video/audio codecs, mux streams package them, and manifests assemble HLS or DASH adaptive playback.
Job templates standardize ladders, overlays, spritesheets and publishing behavior across a media catalog.
applicationFit: Use for uploaded video-on-demand processing, mezzanine conversion and multi-rendition publishing.
Create reusable templates for known device ladders; use per-job configuration only when assets genuinely differ.
Use Live Stream API for real-time feeds and Video Stitcher API for server-side ad personalization.

architectureFlows.title: VOD publishing pipeline
architectureFlows.note: An upload event creates an idempotent job whose renditions are validated before catalog publication.

architectureFlows.title: Controlled template factory
architectureFlows.note: Media engineering versions a standard template and promotion process instead of embedding encoder settings in every application.

security: Grant the Transcoder service agent scoped read/write access to designated buckets; separate template editors from job submitters.
Keep source and output buckets private and deliver through signed CDN/application paths where media is protected.
Validate user-supplied media and job parameters to prevent arbitrary bucket reads/writes or resource-exhaustion abuse.
operations: Track job state, queue time, processing errors, output completeness and quality metrics; emit completion events instead of polling aggressively.
Use deterministic job IDs/output prefixes and record source generation so retries do not overwrite unrelated renditions.
Version templates and validate players, captions and audio tracks before production promotion.
watchPoints: Input/output buckets and job location must meet regional requirements; moving large mezzanine files adds delay and transfer cost.
Successful job status does not guarantee subjective quality or that every target player supports the chosen codecs.
Transcoder does not serve media or manage viewers; Cloud Storage/CDN/player layers remain required.
cost: Charges depend on output duration, resolution and processing features; every rendition increases encoded minutes.
Cloud Storage, event orchestration, CDN and egress are separate.
Avoid unnecessary ladder rungs and re-encoding unchanged assets; retain a high-quality mezzanine for future formats.
alternatives: Transcoder API — Asynchronous file-based VOD transcoding.
Live Stream API — Continuous live-feed transcoding and packaging.
Video Stitcher API — Dynamic ad insertion into existing live/VOD content.

comparisons.fit: Asynchronous file-based VOD transcoding.

comparisons.name: Live Stream API
comparisons.fit: Continuous live-feed transcoding and packaging.

comparisons.fit: Dynamic ad insertion into existing live/VOD content.

Templates standardize ladders and make jobs reproducible.

services.summary: Cloud Translation provides neural text and document translation, language detection, glossaries and custom models for multilingual applications.
concepts: Basic and Advanced editions expose different resources and features; Advanced uses regional locations and supports glossaries, document translation and custom models.
Glossaries bias approved term mappings such as product names; they do not retrain the underlying model.
Synchronous text translation suits small requests, while batch/document methods use Cloud Storage for larger asynchronous workloads.
applicationFit: Use general models for broad language coverage and glossaries for controlled terminology.
Use custom translation models when parallel domain corpora justify training and measurable evaluation.
Use a generative model only when translation is part of a broader reasoning task and nondeterminism is acceptable.

architectureFlows.title: Localized content pipeline
architectureFlows.note: Source content is extracted, translated with a glossary and reviewed before localized publishing.

architectureFlows.title: Batch document translation
architectureFlows.note: Documents move through regional buckets and asynchronous jobs while formatting and outputs are validated.

security: Restrict glossary, model and bucket access; translated output has the same classification as the source.
Avoid sending unnecessary personal or confidential data and choose locations that satisfy residency requirements.
Protect placeholders, markup and control tokens before translation so output cannot alter executable templates or policies.
operations: Evaluate BLEU/COMET plus human quality for important language pairs; monitor language-detection errors and glossary misses.
Version glossaries and custom models with content releases, and maintain fallback behavior for unsupported languages.
Retry batch operations idempotently and preserve source/output manifests for completeness checks.
watchPoints: Automatic language detection can confuse short or mixed-language text; specify source language when known.
Glossary behavior depends on language pair and tokenization; it is terminology guidance, not a universal replacement engine.
Machine translation is unsuitable as the sole authority for legal, clinical or safety-critical text without qualified review.
cost: Text translation is billed by processed characters; document/batch and custom model usage have separate meters.
Storage, human review, orchestration and egress add cost.
Deduplicate identical strings, use translation memory and avoid retranslating unchanged content.
alternatives: Cloud Translation — Purpose-built text/document translation with glossaries.
Custom Translation — Domain-adapted model trained on parallel examples.
Gemini model — Broader multilingual generation and reasoning with different control characteristics.

comparisons.fit: Purpose-built text/document translation with glossaries.

comparisons.name: Custom Translation
comparisons.fit: Domain-adapted model trained on parallel examples.

comparisons.fit: Broader multilingual generation and reasoning with different control characteristics.

memoryHooks: Glossary controls terms; custom model learns from parallel data.
Known language beats auto-detect for short strings.
Exam clue: multilingual text/documents with terminology consistency.

services.summary: An API that annotates stored or streaming video with labels, shots, explicit-content signals, text, objects, speech and other time-based metadata.
concepts: Annotation requests select explicit features; results attach entities and segments to time offsets rather than returning a single image label.
Asynchronous file analysis reads video from Cloud Storage, while streaming annotation targets supported real-time features.
Shot-change detection divides a video into coherent segments that can improve downstream indexing, thumbnails and feature interpretation.
applicationFit: Use for catalog enrichment, moderation assistance, media search and extracting time-aligned metadata from video.
Choose only needed annotation features to control latency, cost and result volume.
Use Agent Platform Vision when managing persistent live streams, application graphs and searchable warehouses.

architectureFlows.title: Media catalog enrichment
architectureFlows.note: A new asset is annotated asynchronously and time-coded metadata becomes searchable alongside the catalog.

architectureFlows.title: Moderation-assistance queue
architectureFlows.note: Explicit-content and object signals prioritize clips for human review without making an automatic final policy decision.

security: Grant read access only to intended source objects and protect annotation output because it can expose transcript and inferred content.
Use human review for moderation or identity-impacting actions; likelihood labels are not determinations.
Apply retention, residency and consent requirements to source media, transcripts and extracted faces/text.
operations: Track long-running operation failures, per-feature latency, annotation volume and quality against a representative media set.
Persist operation IDs and source object generations so retries and catalog updates are idempotent.
Monitor API quotas and split very large catalogs into controllable batches with dead-letter handling.
watchPoints: Feature support, file limits and regional endpoints differ; validate the exact annotation combination.
Time offsets and confidence need downstream tolerance; labels can overlap and vary across model revisions.
Face detection is not face recognition and must not be presented as identity verification.
cost: Billing is based on video minutes and requested annotation features; selecting multiple features compounds processing.
Cloud Storage, eventing, indexing and egress are additional.
Avoid repeatedly annotating identical object generations and store reusable results.
alternatives: Video Intelligence API — Time-based annotations for video files or supported streams.
Vision API — Analysis of individual images and pages.
Agent Platform Vision — Persistent live-video applications and warehouse search.

comparisons.fit: Time-based annotations for video files or supported streams.

comparisons.name: Vision API
comparisons.fit: Analysis of individual images and pages.

comparisons.fit: Persistent live-video applications and warehouse search.

Select only required features; store results by source generation.

services.summary: A server-side ad insertion service that creates personalized HLS/DASH playback sessions by stitching ad decisions into live or video-on-demand manifests.
concepts: A live or VOD session binds source video configuration, ad-tag information and playback parameters, returning a session-specific manifest URI.
The API manipulates manifests so ads and content play as one stream; it does not transcode the underlying program or act as the ad decision server.
CDN keys, slates, ad tracking and session metadata handle delivery integrity and measurement around the stitched manifest.
applicationFit: Use for server-side ad insertion where client ad blockers and seamless playback make manifest-level stitching valuable.
Pair with Live Stream API for managed live outputs or with existing HLS/DASH VOD origins.
Use client-side ad SDKs when interactive ad behavior or client-specific measurement outweighs seamless server-side insertion.

architectureFlows.title: Monetized live channel
architectureFlows.note: A viewer creates a session, the stitcher obtains an ad decision and returns a personalized manifest delivered through the CDN.

architectureFlows.title: VOD ad insertion
architectureFlows.note: A VOD asset and ad tag produce a session-specific timeline while content remains in the existing origin.

security: Authenticate session creation and prevent clients from substituting arbitrary ad tags or source configurations.
Protect CDN keys and origin access; separate configuration administration from application session creation.
Treat ad identifiers and playback events as user data subject to consent, minimization and retention policies.
operations: Monitor session-creation latency, fill rate, manifest errors, ad-media compatibility, beacon delivery and fallback slate use.
Validate ad creatives against codec, duration and rendition requirements before campaigns start.
Use synthetic players across target devices to catch manifest or discontinuity problems before traffic peaks.
watchPoints: Video Stitcher personalizes manifests; it does not create the live channel, host the player or make ad-auction decisions.
Ad creative encoding mismatches can break playback even when session creation succeeds.
Caching must preserve session personalization—do not share a personalized manifest across viewers.
cost: Charges follow stitched playback/session usage; ad decisioning, transcoding, CDN delivery and egress are separate.
Unfilled breaks and invalid creatives affect revenue even if infrastructure cost is low.
Control session churn and select CDN caching rules that reuse segments without caching personalized manifests incorrectly.
alternatives: Video Stitcher API — Server-side personalized ad insertion into manifests.
Live Stream API — Creates live adaptive renditions but not personalized ads.
Transcoder API — Creates VOD renditions and assets, not playback sessions.

services.summary: A pre-trained image analysis API for labels, OCR, landmarks, logos, faces, objects, crop hints and safe-search signals without training a custom model.
concepts: AnnotateImage requests can ask for multiple feature types; each returns independent detections, coordinates and confidence/likelihood values.
Images can be sent as bytes or referenced in Cloud Storage; asynchronous batch file annotation supports supported PDF/TIFF workflows.
Document Text Detection returns page/block/paragraph/word structure, while Text Detection is optimized for text in general images.
applicationFit: Use for commodity image understanding and OCR when pretrained features meet the requirement.
Use Document AI for structured forms/invoices and normalized business entities.
Use a custom Vertex AI vision model when organization-specific classes or domain accuracy require training.

architectureFlows.title: Secure image moderation assist
architectureFlows.note: An upload is isolated, scanned and annotated before policy logic determines publish/review/reject.

architectureFlows.title: OCR indexing pipeline
architectureFlows.note: Images or page files are annotated and structured text is indexed with source coordinates.

security: Restrict object and annotation access; extracted text and inferred attributes can be as sensitive as the image.
Do not use face detection as identity recognition, and avoid fully automated consequential decisions from likelihood scores.
Apply consent, retention, regional and audit requirements to biometric-adjacent and document-image workloads.
operations: Measure feature-specific precision/recall, OCR character error, latency and quota errors using representative images.
Key stored results by object generation and API/model context to avoid stale annotations after image replacement.
Handle partial feature errors independently and route uncertain results for review rather than discarding the whole request.
watchPoints: SafeSearch values are likelihood categories, not policy decisions.
Requesting more features increases latency, output size and cost even when the application ignores them.
Image size, format and batch limits differ across online and file annotation methods.
cost: Billing follows image/page units per requested feature; multiple features on one image are separately metered.
Cloud Storage, orchestration, review and downstream indexing add charges.
Resize where acceptable, request only required features and cache annotations by immutable object version.
alternatives: Vision API — Pretrained general image features and OCR.
Document AI — Layout-aware structured document extraction.
Video Intelligence API — Time-based annotation across video.
Custom vision model — Domain-specific classes trained on labeled examples.
